name: Andromeda
introduction: is named after the princess of Greek myth, daughter of Cassiopeia and Cepheus, who was chained to a rock as a sacrifice to the sea monster Cetus until Perseus rescued her. Her stars form a long chain stretching from the Great Square of Pegasus toward Perseus, best seen on autumn evenings in the Northern Hemisphere.

sections.title: What makes it special
paragraphs: Andromeda is home to the most distant object most people can see with the naked eye: the Andromeda Galaxy, M31, about 2.5 million light-years away. On a dark night it appears as an elongated smudge; its light left the galaxy before our own species existed.

For centuries it was thought to be a nebula within the Milky Way. In 1923, Edwin Hubble found a Cepheid variable star in it, whose pulsation revealed its enormous distance. That discovery showed that the Milky Way is just one galaxy among many.

Andromeda is approaching us at about 110 kilometers per second. Some time in the next several billion years, the two galaxies may collide and merge, although recent studies give this only about even odds.

sections.title: Notable stars
paragraphs: [Sirrah](hip:677), also called Alpheratz, marks the princess’s head and one corner of the Great Square of Pegasus. It was once counted in both constellations. Spectra show it is unusually rich in mercury and manganese.
[Mirach](hip:5447) is a red giant about 200 light-years away. From Mirach, hop north to [Mu Andromedae](hip:4436), then [Nu Andromedae](hip:3881), and the Andromeda Galaxy lies just beyond.
[Almach](hip:9640), at the princess’s foot, is one of the most beautiful double stars in a small telescope: a golden primary with a blue companion. In fact, it is a system of at least four stars.

sections.title: Beyond the stars
paragraphs: The Andromeda Galaxy is escorted by its own satellite galaxies, M32 and M110. Closer to home are the Blue Snowball, NGC 7662, a planetary nebula, and Upsilon Andromedae, in 1999 the first star like the Sun found to host more than one planet.
